data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The dilemma dissolves if we view corroboration not as a measure of truth or probability, but as a measure of informational content and risk. We prefer the better-corroborated theory because it is the most informative theory that has not yet been shown false. The 'cost' is abandoning the goal of certainty or high probability entirely; we choose the boldest, most risky conjecture that survives, knowing it is likely false in detail but offers the highest potential for learning through its eventual falsification.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the goal of science is practical application rather than knowledge growth, this mechanism fails to justify preference for risky theories over safe, tautological ones.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'informational content' cannot be distinguished from 'logical probability' in the limit.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Preference is driven by the desire to maximize information growth. A highly corroborated theory has high empirical content (it forbids much). Choosing it maximizes the exposure to potential falsification in the next round of testing. We do not choose it because we think it is 'true' (induction) or 'probable' (Bayesianism), but because it is the most fertile ground for generating new knowledge via its inevitable failure.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
